edges.description: The complementation arm is the causality argument for this disease. It tests the candidate gene against the biochemical phenotype inside the patient's own genetic background, so it is not vulnerable to the objection that some other variant in that genome caused the enzyme defect.
edges.limitations: Fibroblasts, not heart or brain, so nothing about tissue selectivity or about the cardiomyopathy is testable here. The rescue also establishes that NDUFB7 is limiting for complex I activity in these cells, not the assembly-level mechanism by which it is limiting; no complexome profile or assembly-intermediate analysis has been reported for this patient.

nodes.description:
Reduced electron transfer through complex I lowers oxidative phosphorylation output, and the tissues that decompensate first are the ones with the highest ATP demand: heart and brain. The clinical picture in the index patient follows that pattern, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy, and the anaerobic compensation shows as lactic acidosis.
The tissue-selectivity reasoning is standard mitochondrial-medicine inference rather than a measurement in this patient, so the node is marked PROVISIONAL. No cardiac or brain tissue enzymology was reported.

nodes.description: Loss or alteration of the accessory subunit NDUFB7 disrupts assembly of mitochondrial complex I and reduces respiratory chain supercomplex formation. A systematic knockout screen across all 31 human complex I accessory subunits established that loss of an individual subunit destabilises partner subunits within its structural module, with 25 strictly required for holoenzyme assembly (PMID:27626371), and blue-native analyses of skin fibroblasts from the second MC1DN39 proband directly confirmed deficient complex I assembly and reduced supercomplex formation (PMID:40025060).

nodes.description: Vitamin and electron-carrier cofactor supplementation (including coenzyme Q10, vitamin B complex / riboflavin, thiamine, and carnitine) used empirically across mitochondrial respiratory-chain disorders. While controlled trials in this ultra-rare genotype do not exist, the surviving compound-heterozygous MC1DN39 proband remained clinically stable on coenzyme Q10 and vitamin B complex therapy following surgical management (PMID:40025060), and the mitochondrial antioxidant mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) ameliorated respiratory and neuronal defects in ndufb7-deficient zebrafish embryos.

nodes.description: NDUFB7 variants primarily disrupt complex I assembly and activity; in the compound-heterozygous patient, Complex III and IV amounts and the I/III/IV supercomplex were secondarily reduced as well. This node is where the causal argument closes for the index patient: expressing wild-type NDUFB7 in the patient's own fibroblasts normalised complex I function, so the enzyme defect is attributable to NDUFB7 and not to an unrelated variant carried by the same patient.

nodes.description:
There is no disease-modifying therapy for MC1DN39, and none for nuclear complex I deficiency generally. Management is symptomatic: treating the lactic acidosis, the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the encephalopathy as they present.
This block records the state of the field rather than a disease-specific treatment response. The second reported MC1DN39 proband remained clinically stable on coenzyme Q10 and vitamin B complex, but that uncontrolled single-patient observation is not evidence for disease-modifying efficacy.

nodes.description: Zebrafish embryos knocked down for ndufb7 develop brain ventricular and neuronal defects, elevated lactic acid levels, and reduced oxygen consumption indicating defective mitochondrial respiration; these defects are partially rescued by ectopic ndufb7 expression and ameliorated by mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ), with only MitoQ rescuing the oxygen-consumption defect.
